Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I've gathered. Here is the commentary:

---

## Judges 6 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; so He delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years"

**Traditional Reading:**
- After forty years of rest following Deborah and Barak's victory (Judg. 5:31), prosperity bred complacency and Israel again fell into idolatry — specifically worshipping the gods of the Amorites (v. 10). The "evil" here is identified as Baal worship. (Gill, studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-6.html; Precept Austin, preceptaustin.org/judges_6_commentary)
- God's act of delivering them to Midian was actually an act of grace: the oppression was designed to turn Israel back to God. It would have been worse if God had simply left them alone in their sin. (Enduring Word, enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-6/)
- The Midianites were descended from Abraham through Keturah (Gen. 25:2) and occupied lands east of the Jordan, near Moab. They had been nearly destroyed by Israel in Moses' time (Num. 31), but by this time — roughly two centuries later — had recovered and become powerful again. (Gill; Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/judges/6.htm)

**Reformed Perspective:**
- Ligonier notes the fundamental problem was not suffering at foreign hands but idolatry; suffering was the consequence of the real issue. God does not always wait for hearts to be right before bringing relief, as seen when He called Gideon. (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-calls-gideon)

---

### v. 2 — "the hand of Midian prevailed against Israel … shelters in the mountains, caves, and strongholds"

**Traditional Reading:**
- The word "prevailed" (Hebrew 'azaz) is the same verb used of Othniel when the Spirit came upon him and he "prevailed" over Cushan-rishathaim (Judg. 3:10) — a tragic reversal: now the enemy prevails because Israel has turned from God. (Precept Austin)
- The "dens" (Hebrew mineharoth) may mean torrent-gullies converted into hiding places, or catacombs and galleries in rocks. Three kinds of refuge are noted: dens/galleries, mountain crags, and limestone caves. This was a return to "troglodyte habits." (Ellicott)
- Charles Spurgeon: "The Lord does not permit His children to sin successfully." (Quoted in Precept Austin)

---

### v. 3 — "Whenever the Israelites would plant their crops, the Midianites, Amalekites, and other people of the east would come up"

**Traditional Reading:**
- The Midianites did not occupy the land year-round but came seasonally at harvest time to steal. The Amalekites (ancient enemies, Ex. 17) joined them, along with "the children of the east" — a general term for Arab tribes (Benî Kedem). (Ellicott; Gill)
- The pattern was especially cruel: they let the Israelites do all the hard work of ploughing and sowing, then swept in to steal the harvest. (Precept Austin; Ellicott)

---

### v. 4 — "encamping against them as far as Gaza and destroying the produce of the land"

**Traditional Reading:**
- The swath of destruction stretched from the Jordan eastward to Gaza on the Mediterranean coast — the entire breadth of the land. They cut down corn, grass, vines, and olives, leaving nothing alive. (Gill; Ellicott; Enduring Word, citing Clarke)
- The Israelites were too weak and impoverished to offer any real resistance; these were not battles but systematic plundering. (Ellicott)
- The Midianites' camels were a devastating new military technology, giving them swift, long-range attack capability against foot-bound Israelites. A camel can travel 300 miles without food or water. (Precept Austin, citing Gary Inrig)

---

### v. 5 — "like a great swarm of locusts … camels were innumerable"

**Traditional Reading:**
- The locust imagery (also used in Judg. 7:12; Joel 2) conveys both number and destructive effect — they consumed everything. Bedouins still call locusts "Gurrud Allah" — "Host of God." (Ellicott)
- Camels were uncommon in Palestine and were brought from eastern deserts. Midian and Arabia were famous for camels (Isa. 60:6). The description "without number" is Oriental hyperbole — a Bedouin asked to count his brothers flung sand in the air saying, "Equally numberless." (Ellicott; Gill)

---

### v. 6 — "Israel was greatly impoverished … and the Israelites cried out to the LORD"

**Traditional Reading:**
- The LXX renders "impoverished" as "reduced to pauperism"; the Hebrew implies flaccidity and helplessness. The people were "made small" agriculturally, economically, and socially. (Ellicott; Precept Austin citing Inrig)
- They "cried out to the LORD" — but David Guzik notes that prayer was their last resort rather than their first resource. Gill adds that they "cried not to the idols they had served, being sensible they could not help them," yet they still did so without true repentance. (Enduring Word; Gill; Precept Austin)
- Precept Austin observes this cry seems to have been more remorse than repentance, because the people were unaware of the moral cause behind their suffering until the prophet pointed it out in vv. 7-10. (preceptaustin.org/judges_6_commentary)

---

### v. 7-8a — "Now when the Israelites cried out … He sent them a prophet"

**Traditional Reading:**
- In previous cycles, God responded to Israel's cry by immediately sending a deliverer (Judg. 3:9). This time He first sends an unnamed prophet — a "man, a prophet" — to confront the real problem before sending the deliverer. (Enduring Word; Precept Austin)
- Jewish tradition (the Seder Olam Rabba) identified this prophet as Phinehas, son of Eleazar, but Gill dismisses this as improbable given the 200+ year gap. We simply do not know his name. (Gill; Ellicott)
- This is one of only two prophets named in the book of Judges (the other being Deborah). God used prophets in isolated cases before the institution of the prophetic order under Samuel. (Precept Austin)

---

### vv. 8b-10 — "I brought you up out of Egypt … But you did not obey Me"

**Traditional Reading:**
- The prophet's message follows the pattern of the covenant lawsuit: (1) recounting God's gracious acts (brought you from Egypt, delivered from oppressors, gave you the land); (2) stating God's command (do not fear the gods of the Amorites); (3) declaring Israel's breach (you did not obey). (Enduring Word; Ellicott; Precept Austin)
- The prophet told Israel where the real problem was: not that Midian was so strong, but that Israel was so disobedient. They were blaming Midianites for problems they themselves had caused. (Enduring Word)
- "The gods of the Amorites" — the Amorites were the most powerful Canaanite tribe, so their name sometimes stands for all Canaanites (Josh. 24:15). (Ellicott)

---

### v. 11 — "the angel of the LORD came and sat down under the oak in Ophrah … Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress"

**Traditional Reading (Theophany view):**
- "The Angel of the LORD" (Maleak-Jehovah) is distinct from the prophet in v. 8 (nabi). Josephus describes the figure as "a phantasm … in the shape of a youth," but the text presents a real appearance. (Ellicott)
- Enduring Word, following David Guzik (a Pentecostal/charismatic teacher), holds this is a theophany — the pre-incarnate Christ appearing in human form. Supporting evidence: the figure is called "the LORD" directly in vv. 14, 16, and 23. Since no one has seen the Father (John 1:18) and the Spirit has no bodily form, this is understood as God the Son. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-6/)
- Ellicott notes the alternative view: the angel speaks only as God's mouthpiece, not as God Himself. But he observes that the text repeatedly switches between "the angel of the LORD" and "the LORD," supporting the theophany reading.
- Threshing wheat in a winepress (a sunken vat) was both difficult and humiliating — wheat was normally threshed on open hilltops so the wind could blow away chaff. Gideon did this secretly, beating grain with a staff rather than using oxen, to avoid Midianite detection. (Gill; Enduring Word; Ellicott)
- Ophrah was in western Manasseh, territory of the Abiezrites (descendants of Abiezer, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh — Josh. 17:2). (Ellicott; Gill)

---

### v. 12 — "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor"

**Traditional Reading:**
- This was a strange greeting. It didn't appear the LORD was with him (he was hiding in a winepress) and he didn't seem a "mighty man of valor." Gideon might have looked around to see if the angel was addressing someone else. (Enduring Word)
- Ellicott suggests Gideon may already have distinguished himself in earlier warfare — possibly the battle against Sisera (Judg. 8:18; 4:6) — making the address not entirely ironic.
- The Targum renders it: "My Word is thy help." (Gill)

**Reformed Perspective:**
- Ligonier notes God's identification of Gideon as a "mighty man of valor" despite his doubts highlights that it is God's calling, not Gideon's inherent qualities, that makes him mighty. (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-calls-gideon)

---

### v. 13 — "Please, my Lord … if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us?"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gideon used the respectful but ordinary title "adoni" ("sir"), not yet recognizing he spoke to a divine being. (Ellicott)
- Gideon's questions reveal he had been deeply meditating on Israel's condition. He knew the stories of the Exodus and the miracles, and the contrast with present oppression troubled him. (Enduring Word; Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary, studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/judges-6.html)
- Yet Gideon's analysis was backward: he thought God had forsaken Israel, when in truth Israel had forsaken God. He saw the problem as divine abandonment rather than national sin. (Enduring Word)

**Baptist Perspective:**
- John Piper (Desiring God) notes Gideon's question — "If the Lord is with us, why has all this happened?" — is the cry of a heart that doubts God's purposes but still reaches toward Him. Piper teaches that we must "reframe" such questions: God's presence does not guarantee ease, and suffering can coexist with His being with us. (desiringgod.org/articles/if-god-is-with-me-why-did-this-happen)

---

### v. 14 — "Go in the strength you have and save Israel … Am I not sending you?"

**Traditional Reading:**
- "Go in this your strength" — what strength? Guzik lists Gideon's hidden strengths: the might of the humble, the caring (he was troubled about Israel), the knowledgeable (he knew God's past works), the spiritually hungry, the teachable, and the weak (2 Cor. 12:9). (Enduring Word)
- The emphasis falls on "Have I not sent you?" — the authority for the mission rests not on Gideon's qualifications but on God's commission. This parallels God's call to Moses (Ex. 3:12). (Enduring Word; Gill)
- Precept Austin stresses that "this your strength" is the strength God has given by promising His presence — God's answer to discouragement is not positive thinking but the promise of His presence. (preceptaustin.org/judges_6_commentary)

---

### v. 15 — "my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father's house"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gideon's protest echoes Moses (Ex. 4:1-13), Saul (1 Sam. 9:21), Isaiah (Isa. 6:5), and Jeremiah (Jer. 1:6-7) — the preliminary diffidence of humility in those God calls. (Ellicott)
- "My family" is literally "my thousand" (the military/clan subdivision). Gideon says his thousand is the meanest in Manasseh. He also claims to be "the least" (possibly the youngest) in his father's house. This is spoken in humility — yet Gideon had ten servants (v. 27), indicating he was not destitute. (Ellicott; Gill)
- Ellicott notes Gideon's brothers had all been slain (Judg. 8:18), making him "the last of his father's house" as well.

---

### v. 16 — "Surely I will be with you … you will strike down all the Midianites as one man"

**Traditional Reading:**
- God's answer is not to build Gideon's self-confidence but to give him God-confidence. The promise "I will be with you" is the same assurance given to Moses (Ex. 3:12) and to all believers (Matt. 28:20). (Enduring Word)
- "As one man" means the Midianites will be struck down all together, as easily as if they were a single person — total and complete victory. (Gill)

---

### vv. 17-18 — "give me a sign … Let me bring my offering … I will stay until you return"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gideon requests a confirming sign. David Guzik argues this was not wrong in principle: when guidance concerns matters not specifically detailed in Scripture, seeking confirmation is legitimate. Gideon needed to know this was truly God speaking before risking everything. (Enduring Word)
- The word Gideon uses for "offering" is minchah — a neutral term that can mean a gift, present, or meal offering. He seems to be cautiously probing: is this visitor merely human (in which case it's hospitality) or divine (in which case it's an offering)? (Ellicott; Gill)
- The angel's agreement to wait ("I will stay until you return") displays remarkable divine condescension. (Gill)

---

### vv. 19-21 — Gideon prepared a young goat, unleavened bread, an ephah of flour … fire flared from the rock

**Traditional Reading:**
- Unleavened cakes were chosen for speed of preparation (as with Lot, Gen. 19:3; the witch of Endor, 1 Sam. 28:24). An ephah of flour (about 22½ lbs) was lavish — far more than one person could eat — reflecting Eastern hospitality. (Ellicott; Gill)
- The angel directed Gideon to lay the food on "this rock" and pour out the broth — treating the rock as an altar and the food as a sacrifice, with the broth poured out as a libation/drink offering (cf. Gen. 35:14; 1 Kings 18:34). (Ellicott)
- Fire rising from the rock to consume the offering is the classic sign of divine acceptance (Lev. 9:24; 1 Kings 18:38; 1 Chron. 21:26; 2 Chron. 7:1). Ellicott notes: "Water is brought out of the rock for the blessing of man, and fire to show the presence of God." (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
- The angel then "vanished from his sight" — unlike Judges 13:20 where the angel ascends in the flame; here the departure is immediate. (Ellicott)

---

### v. 22 — "Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Only now does Gideon fully realize the identity of the visitor. Before this, he believed he was speaking with a man. The angel's human appearance was complete. (Enduring Word)
- Gideon's terror reflects the universal ancient belief — shared by Israel and pagans alike — that seeing a divine being would bring death (cf. Judg. 13:22; Gen. 16:13; 32:30; Ex. 33:20; Isa. 6:5). Callimachus wrote, "Whosoever … looks on any of the immortals, sees them only to his own great cost." (Ellicott)
- Charles Spurgeon noted: "Why was Gideon afraid? Not because he was a coward … but because even brave men are alarmed at the supernatural." (Quoted in Enduring Word)

---

### vv. 23-24 — "Peace be with you. Do not be afraid … Gideon built an altar … The LORD Is Peace"

**Traditional Reading:**
- God's word of peace calms Gideon's terror. This echoes other divine reassurances (Dan. 10:19; Ezek. 2:1; Luke 1:13; Rev. 1:17). (Ellicott)
- The altar named "Jehovah-shalom" ("The LORD Is Peace") was built not primarily for sacrifice but as a memorial to this divine encounter and the peace God gave. This follows the pattern of other named altars: Jehovah-jireh (Gen. 22:14), Jehovah-nissi (Ex. 17:15). (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
- Spurgeon preached: "When Gideon is fully at peace, what does he begin to do for God? … Our Lord came to give us peace that he might send us out to war." (Quoted in Enduring Word)
- The phrase "to this day it stands in Ophrah" indicates the altar was still known when the book of Judges was written. (Ellicott)

---

### vv. 25-27 — "Take your father's young bull … tear down your father's altar to Baal … cut down the Asherah pole"

**Traditional Reading:**
- The command came "on that very night" — immediately. God's guidance came swiftly once Gideon was responsive. Reformation at home had to precede national deliverance: God told Gideon to get his own house in order first. (Enduring Word)
- Ellicott observes: "It was distinctly revealed to Gideon that he must be an iconoclast before he could be a deliverer." (Ellicott)
- The "two bulls" have been interpreted variously. Gill suggests one was for a sin offering, the other for consecration. Clarke noted the second bull was seven years old, matching the length of the Midianite oppression — its death symbolised the end of their slavery. (Enduring Word citing Clarke; Gill)
- Luther is cited as saying divine communication here was not a voice in the air but an unmistakable inner revelation. (Ellicott)
- The Asherah pole was a wooden pillar representing the Canaanite goddess Asherah/Ashtoreth, associated with sensual fertility rites. These were not trees but carved columns. (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary)
- Gideon obeyed — but "by night rather than in the daytime, because he was too afraid." His fear of men still exceeded his fear of the Lord. (Enduring Word; Ligonier)

**Reformed Perspective:**
- Ligonier notes this was essential: "Yahweh, the one true creator God, will tolerate no competitors. Israelites can have Yahweh as their Savior or they can have Baal as their 'deliverer,' but they cannot have both (see also Matt. 6:24)." Gideon's fear shows "his fear of men is still greater than his fear of the Lord." (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-calls-gideon)

---

### vv. 28-30 — "the men of the city … 'Bring out your son. He must die'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- The townspeople quickly identified Gideon as the culprit. The demand for death shows how entrenched Baal worship was. Wolf is cited: "The heresy had become the main religion." (Enduring Word)
- Baal was worshipped as the god of weather and agricultural fertility. In the hard economic times caused by Midianite raids, people doubled down on Baal worship instead of turning to Yahweh — making their situation worse. Clarke noted Baal and Ashtaroth attracted more worshippers because "their rites were more adapted to the fallen nature of man." (Enduring Word citing Clarke)

---

### vv. 31-32 — Joash: "Are you contending for Baal? … If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself"

**Traditional Reading:**
- Joash's defense of his son is brilliantly logical: if Baal is truly a god, he can defend his own altar — he doesn't need human advocates. This argument shamed the crowd into silence and saved Gideon's life. (Enduring Word; Ellicott; Garner-Howes)
- Joash's response may indicate his own turning from Baal: "Here is a very good example. Gideon was strengthened to undertake the Lord's battle, which made his father forsake Baal and line up with him." (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary)
- The nickname "Jerubbaal" means "Let Baal contend against him" — originally a taunt from the Baal-worshippers that became a title of honour. Trapp called it "a title of honour." (Enduring Word; Ellicott)

---

### vv. 33-35 — "the Midianites … camped in the Valley of Jezreel … the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon"

**Traditional Reading:**
- The enemy coalition — Midianites, Amalekites, and eastern peoples — crossed the Jordan and encamped in the Valley of Jezreel (also called Esdraelon), a broad fertile plain near the border of Manasseh and Issachar, and significant as the future site of Armageddon. (Garner-Howes; Pulpit Commentary, studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/judges-6.html)
- "The Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon" (literally "clothed" him) — this follows the Old Covenant pattern where the Spirit comes upon specific individuals for specific purposes of divinely-empowered leadership. Under the New Covenant, the Spirit is poured out on all flesh (Joel 2:28-29; Acts 2:17-18). (Enduring Word)
- Gideon blew the trumpet (shofar/ram's horn) and rallied the Abiezrites, then sent messengers throughout Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali — the northern tribes. Notably, three of these (Zebulun, Naphtali, and now Asher) had fought under Barak. The Pulpit Commentary observes it is "pleasing to see Asher now joined with them instead of abiding in his breaches." (Pulpit Commentary)
- Judges 7:3 later tells us 32,000 men assembled. (Enduring Word)

---

### vv. 36-38 — The Fleece: first test — fleece wet, ground dry

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gideon had already received one miraculous sign (the fire from the rock, vv. 17-21). Yet now, facing battle, he asks for a second — then a third — confirming sign. This was weak, imperfect faith. David Guzik writes: "For such a bold, life-endangering mission, one might understand his request for one sign … But asking for second and third signs showed that his faith was weak." (Enduring Word)
- Yet Guzik also urges caution: "Many of us would immediately refuse such a call, without even considering allowing God to confirm it. Gideon's weak faith was still greater than no faith. For this reason, Gideon is rightly included in … Hebrews 11:32." (Enduring Word)
- Gideon also did not keep his word — he said one sign would suffice, then asked for another. God was merciful and gracious despite this. Wood is cited: "This is an outstanding example of God's gracious patience with a troubled child." (Enduring Word)
- The Pulpit Commentary speculates that heavy night dews on the hill of Gilead (where Gideon was encamped, possibly Mount Gilboa), together with sheep-skins used as protection against cold nights, may have suggested this particular test. (Pulpit Commentary)

**Reformed Perspective:**
- Ligonier teaches that Gideon's request for the fleece sign "evidences his half-hearted faith." Gideon didn't doubt God's existence or power — he was uncertain the Lord "actually would help him." God's word should have been sufficient. The sign was granted graciously because defeating Midian was essential for preserving the messianic line (Gen. 22:17-18; Gal. 3:15-16). Ligonier warns: "We should not think, however, that the Lord will send us extrabiblical signs as a matter of course … We must be content with the direction God gives us in Scripture." (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gideon-and-fleece)

---

### vv. 39-40 — The Fleece: second test — fleece dry, ground wet

**Traditional Reading:**
- Gideon's preface — "Do not be angry with me; let me speak one more time" — shows he knew he was pushing the limits of propriety. Yet God graciously granted this second (cumulatively third) sign. (Enduring Word; Gill)
- The opposite nature of the two signs — first the fleece wet/ground dry, then fleece dry/ground wet — ensured this was unmistakably supernatural. Normally, whatever is left outside gets wet when dew falls. (Ligonier, as summarized above)

**Traditional typological reading (Gill, citing "many interpreters"):**
- Gill reports a common traditional interpretation: "all this is an emblem of the different case and state of the Jews and Gentiles under the different dispensations." Under the Old Covenant, Israel alone (the fleece) received the dew of divine favour while the Gentile world was dry; under the New Covenant, the Gentiles receive abundant blessing while the Jews are "entirely destitute of them." (Gill)
- Enduring Word also mentions Origen's allegorical reading: the fleece represents the Jewish people, the surrounding area the Gentiles; the fleece wet while ground dry pictures God's favour on Israel alone; then the fleece dry with ground wet pictures the Gentile church receiving the Spirit's outpouring. (Enduring Word)

**Contemporary Application Note:**
- Christians sometimes speak of "putting out a fleece" — seeking a sign from God for guidance. Most teachers across traditions caution that this was Gideon's weakness, not a model to emulate, and that we now have the full counsel of Scripture to guide us. (Enduring Word; Ligonier)

---

### Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**Identity of "the Angel of the LORD" (vv. 11-24):**
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word/David Guzik): Unequivocally a theophany — the pre-incarnate Christ. This is the standard conservative charismatic reading.
- **Anglican** (Ellicott): Acknowledges both views. Notes the text "has been hence inferred that this angel was no created angel, but 'the angel of the covenant.'" But also notes the alternative — the angel speaks as God's mouthpiece.
- **Reformed** (Ligonier): "The angel of the Lord Himself appears to Gideon" — affirms the divine identity without dogmatic specification about the Second Person.

**The Fleece as a Model for Decision-Making (vv. 36-40):**
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic stream**: More open to the idea that God may grant circumstantial signs. David Guzik says seeking confirmation "in regard to something as life-or-death as leading Israel into battle … it is possible to look for and expect confirmation in various ways" — while still acknowledging Gideon's weak faith.
- **Reformed** (Ligonier): Strongly rejects fleece-laying as a model. "We should not think … the Lord will send us extrabiblical signs as a matter of course … We must be content with the direction God gives us in Scripture."
- **Baptist** (Garner-Howes): "In some respects it might seem commendable that Gideon wished to be absolutely certain … although it seems his faith was somewhat lacking." A middle position — understanding the motive but not endorsing the method.

**Gideon's Character — Hero or Antihero?**
- **Reformed** (Ligonier): Describes Gideon as "the least exemplary of the judges so far" — emphasising his doubts, his need for multiple signs, and his fear of men.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word): More sympathetic — "Gideon's weak faith was still greater than no faith … Gideon is rightly included in … Hebrews 11:32."
- **Baptist** (Garner-Howes): Lists Gideon's godly qualities — a man of meditation, the Word, prayer, and humility — presenting a positive assessment.

---

### Other Views Noted

**Modern Scholarship (from Ellicott's allusions):**
- Ellicott notes the "minute and unexplained detail" of the "second bullock" as evidence "that we are not moving in the region of legend" — an implicit argument for the historical reliability of the narrative against critical scholarship that might treat it as myth. (Ellicott)

**Catholic and Orthodox Readings:**
- Unfortunately, search results from newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org were not retrieved in time. (The search limit was reached.)

**Gill's typological reading (vv. 37-40):**
- The two fleece signs as an emblem of the two covenants and the shift of divine favour from Jews to Gentiles represents a traditional Reformed/Baptist typological approach common in older commentaries. (Gill)
